title: Understand static variables through LanguageLab state
answer: A static variable belongs to the class itself rather than to each individual object instance. There is one class-level copy associated with the loaded class, and all instances access that shared state. Static fields are commonly used for constants, counters, caches, configuration shared at the class level, or other data that logically belongs to the type rather than one object. In `LanguageLab`, `private static int batches` is shared across all `LanguageLab` instances, while `accepted` is an instance field with a separate value per object. The `VALID` and `GROUND` fields are `public static final` constants. Static mutable state should be used carefully because shared access can create concurrency and test-isolation concerns.

steps.question: Static avoids one copy per instance, while final prevents the constant from being reassigned. The `VALID` and `GROUND` flags are declared `public static final`, combining class-level ownership with immutability after initialization. steps.why: Static avoids one copy per instance, while final prevents the constant from being reassigned.
steps.why_te: Highlight ayina line ni chudandi. `static` valla constants class ki belong avutayi, prathi object ki separate copy avasaram ledu. `final` valla initialization taruvata values reassign cheyyaleru.

steps.why: An instance field would give each LanguageLab object its own independent batches value rather than one shared counter.
